newsitem.title: USA: Drug trial, new surgery featured at heart meeting.
newsitem.headline: Drug trial, new surgery featured at heart meeting.

text.p: Results from a huge trial testing a new heart drug, studies on blood clot fighters and minimally invasive heart surgery will be featured at this week's annual meeting of the American Heart Association.

The association said it expects more than 33,000 cardiologists, scientists and other health care workers to attend its four-day scientific sessions that starts Sunday in New Orleans. Some 360 companies will be discussing their cardiovascular drugs and devices at the meeting.
One of the features of the meeting will be a study unveiled Wednesday involving 19,000 patients across 16 countries testing the effect of the drug clopidogrel versus aspirin.
A spokeswoman from Bristol-Myers Squibb Co., which is co-developing clopidogrel with France's Sanofi, described the trial as largest ever done on a drug in development.
Pharmaceutical industry analysts said the trial is particularily difficult because it is testing the drug against an active ingredient, aspirin, rather than against a placebo.
It is also testing its ability to prevent three conditions -- heart attack, stroke and periperhal vascular disease -- better than aspirin.
"If the results are very robust, it's all the more significant because the study was such a hard one to do," said Stephen Scala, an analyst at Cowen & Co.
If the study does show strong results, analysts said they expect Bristol-Myers to file clopidogrel for Food and Drug Administration approval in early 1997.
Among biotechnology features at the meeting will be six-month data on a trial of Centocor Inc.'s blood-clot fighting drug ReoPro.
Interventional cardiologists, with a traditional preference to devices over drugs, have been slow in adopting the drug since its launch in early 1995, analysts said.
The study on the drug's use in patients receiving angioplasty could help Centocor, and its ReoPro partner Eli Lilly & Co., sway doctors, analysts said.

"As the data comes out more and more, and is more and more powerfully in Centocor's favour, I think it will be tough for anybody to argue" against the drug, said Lisa Tuckerman, a biotechnology analyst at Spears, Benzak, Salomon and Farrell.
Data on a rival blood-clot fighting drug, COR Therapeutics Inc. and Schering-Plough Corp.'s Integrelin, will also be presented at the conference.
Cardiologists will also be shown studies on a new technique known as minimally invasive heart surgery, in which surgeons work through small holes in the chest, instead of cutting the chest open.
Companies working in the field include Heartport Inc., CardioThoracic Systems Inc. and Medtronic Inc.
